title: Coarsening at random for multiple instance learning: identifiability conditions for instance-level inference
description:
Multiple instance learning (MIL) trains on bags of instances labelled only at the bag level: a bag is positive when at least one of its instances is positive, and the instance labels are latent. Methods such as mi-SVM, Diverse Density, and attention-based deep MIL recover instance-level structure, but the conditions under which instance-level inference is identifiable from bag labels have not been characterized. We show that MIL is an instance of the masked-data identifiability problem from reliability statistics: instances are components, bags are candidate sets, the 'at least one positive instance' rule is series (logical-OR) aggregation, and singleton bags (instance-level labels) are singleton candidate sets that restore identifiability.

We establish: (i) a rank condition for identifiability of instance-type positivity, stated in terms of the bag-by-instance-type composition matrix, together with its continuous-feature extension in terms of the bag-summed feature matrix; (ii) a bag-prevalence consistency theorem showing that any interior bag-likelihood maximizer satisfies an IRLS-weighted moment-matching identity along the column space of the composition matrix, so bag-level accuracy cannot validate instance-level scores; and (iii) a closed-form first-order bias bound under aggregation-rule misspecification. The standard-versus-collective MIL assumption taxonomy is recovered as a statement about which aggregation rules preserve the support (C1) coarsening condition, and a confound between intrinsic instance positivity and the noisy-OR firing rate is identified as the discrete-label analogue of the spike-in capture-efficiency gap in scRNA-seq.

A multi-seed simulation confirms the three theorems with known instance-level ground truth, and an application to the MUSK1 and MUSK2 benchmarks demonstrates the rank diagnostic and the boundary-MLE regime on real chemical-descriptor data. The continuous-feature refit, including a PCA rank-reduction prescribed by the rank theorem, shows that restoring identifiability stabilizes estimation but does not by itself buy predictive competitiveness, cleanly separating the identifiability axis from the model-class axis.
